title: The protection system
hookLine: the Khalsa offered villages protection in return for a share of the harvest

cards: Harvest time in a Punjab village, in the hard years. The wheat is in, and everyone knows what can come next: raiders, a local strongman's men, tax collectors who take far more than the tax.
There's no police to call, and the government in Lahore is either far away or part of the problem. Then Sikh horsemen ride in, and their leader makes the village elders an offer.
Pay us a share of the harvest, and no one touches this village. If anyone does, they answer to us. That offer has a name: rakhi.

teach.b: Rakhi is Punjabi for guarding, keeping watch, protection; in these years it became the name of a system. A Sikh band, tradition says, took a village under its rakhi.

teach.h: A SHARE OF THE HARVEST FOR SAFETY.
teach.b: The village paid a share of its crops at harvest, and the band promised to keep it safe from plunder, by anyone. Only a few years earlier, this community had lived in the forests with a price on its head.

The hunted were becoming the protectors. Tradition says villagers who had never taken amrit, Hindu and Muslim as well as Sikh, now looked to the Khalsa to keep their harvest safe. It isn't a simple story.
Some readers see in rakhi an early shape of the Sikh states to come: protection, then loyalty, then land.
Some point out that a band collecting a share for safety holds real power over a village, and power can be used well or badly. Sikh tradition remembers the ideal and measures the bands against it.

Where does that ideal come from? The Sikh scripture keeps describing God as the protector, the keeper, the shelter of those who have no shelter. And Sikh teaching holds that the Khalsa is there to defend the weak.

A line of Guru Arjan, in paraphrase, says the Lord has become the protector, and no one can harm the one he keeps. Rakhi made that an everyday job: walking a village's boundary, answering when someone called for help.
Sikhs today don't collect a harvest share, but the job survives in a smaller shape: knowing your neighbors, and being someone they could come to.

how: Sikhs speak of the Khalsa's duty to protect the weak, and Sikh groups today organize practical help for neighbors in need, regardless of faith.

o: a festival thanking God for a safe harvest in the village
a tax every village owed the governor in Lahore at harvest
protection: guarding a village in return for a harvest share

games.q: the protection system — tap the pairs.

s: villages under rakhi were all Sikh villages
tradition says Hindu and Muslim villagers also came under the Khalsa's rakhi.
in return for protection, a village paid a share of its harvest
that share was the price of keeping the village safe from plunder.
rakhi was simple charity, with no power involved
a band that collected a share for safety held real power over a village, and some readers see an early shape of later Sikh states in it.

games.q: you're an elder in a Punjab village. raiders could come any harvest, and Lahore won't help. a Sikh band offers protection for a share of the crop. what do you do?
o: refuse, and hope the raiders pass you by.
accept, and take the village under their rakhi.
pay the raiders instead, to keep them away.
games.why: tradition says villages accepted, and the Khalsa that had been hunted became the guard on the village boundary.

practice: In your mind, walk the boundary of your own small village, your street, your building, your team, and notice one person who might need a little looking after.
Picture one small way to keep watch, a knock, a message, a carried bag, and if you pray, hold them in mind and say Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Rakhi. Protection. The system in which Sikh bands guarded villages from plunder in return for a share of the harvest. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: rakhi, guarding or protection; here the name of the eighteenth-century system of Sikh protection for villages.

carryVoice: Your line: keep the village safe. A promise kept one harvest at a time. Day eight hundred fifty-eight, done.
